title: Derivative of the product density derivative
statement: Let $I$ be a finite index set, let $v\ge0$, and let $c,z\in\mathbb R^I$. The function of $m\in\mathbb R^I$ given by the derivative of the product Gaussian density at mean $m$ is differentiable at $c$. Its derivative, applied to directions $h,k\in\mathbb R^I$, is $G_v(c,z)\bigl(S_v(c,z)[h]S_v(c,z)[k]-\sum_{i\in I}h_i k_i/v\bigr)$, where $G_v$ is the product Gaussian density, $S_v(c,z)[h]=\sum_i((z_i-c_i)/v)h_i$, and division by zero is interpreted as zero.
replaced: Let $I$ be finite and $v\ge0$. Put $G_v(c,z)=\prod_i p_v(c_i,z_i)$, where $p_v$ is the Gaussian density of variance $v$ for $v>0$ and $p_0=0$, and put $S_v(c,z)[h]=\sum_i((z_i-c_i)/v)h_i$, with division by zero equal to zero. Define $A_v(c,z)[h]=G_v(c,z)S_v(c,z)[h]$ and $T_v(c,z)[h,k]=G_v(c,z)(S_v(c,z)[h]S_v(c,z)[k]-\sum_i h_i k_i/v)$. For all $c,z\in\mathbb R^I$, the derivative at $c$ of $m\mapsto A_v(m,z)$ is $T_v(c,z)$.
